nodes.statement: The Wick ordering () is crucial in Theorem , as our solution has infinite mass when s_pr<s<0; in this case the Wick-ordered NLS, rather than the original one, is the right equation to study. In fact, even in the simplest case (d,p)=(1,3), the NLS without the renormalization as in Remark will have no solution for any infinite mass initial data; see . As another example, for the dynamical Phi_2^4 model (2D cubic heat equation with white noise forcing), the canonical smooth approximations will converge to a nontrivial limit only with Wick ordering, otherwise the limit would be identically zero for any initial condition (see ).
nodes.raw_latex: \label{needwick} The Wick ordering (\ref{wickpoly}) is crucial in Theorem \ref{main}, as our solution has infinite mass when $s_{pr}<s<0$; in this case the Wick-ordered NLS, rather than the original one, is the right equation to study. In fact, even in the simplest case $(d,p)=(1,3)$, the NLS without the renormalization as in Remark \ref{1dcubic} will have \emph{no solution} for \emph{any} infinite mass initial data; see \cite{GO}. As another example, for the dynamical $\Phi_2^4$ model (2D cubic heat equation with white noise forcing), the canonical smooth approximations will converge to a nontrivial limit only with Wick ordering, otherwise the limit would be identically zero for any initial condition (see \cite{ChW,HR+}).

nodes.statement: Although Theorem concerns singular (i.e. low regularity) data and short-time solutions, the fundamental issue here is to understand how the randomness structurefootnoteSuch structure lives on high frequencies and fine scales. It becomes more explicit when considering low regularity solutions, and may be obscured by the dominant coarse scale profile in high regularity solutions. propagates under the nonlinear Schr\"odinger flow. With this understanding, we can easily obtain new results for regular data and long-time solutions, such as Theorem below.

Even in the H^1 subcritical case where u_ho exists for all time, Theorem demonstrates the highly nontrivial fact that there is no significant energy shift (such as a cascade) in u_ho, (almost) until this very long time T=N^(p-1)(s-s_pr). In comparison, for deterministic data, say when g_k(omega) in () are replaced by 1, one can describe the asymptotic behavior of u_ho only up to timefootnoteIn fact there is energy shift in u_ho at time N^(p-1)(s-s_cr), dictated by the continuous resonance (CR) equation; see . Note that, the approximation leading to the CR equation does not work in our case as randomization destroys the differentiability in rescaled Fourier space; in fact the solution u_ho in Theorem has no energy shift at this time. It is currently unknown whether the solution u_ho in Theorem , or the corresponding ensemble average, satisfies some effective equation at time N^(p-1)(s-s_pr). O(N^(p-1)(s-s_cr)) provided s>s_cr; see for the p=3 case. Therefore, the randomization () effectively extends the time of perturbative regime for the given homogeneous initial data. In essence, this is the same as Theorem , where we keep the time of perturbative regime constant (namely 1), and randomization allows us to increase the size of initial data at a given frequency (equivalent to reducing regularity).

When $s_{cr}>1$, i.e. (\ref{nls}) is $H^1$ supercritical in the usual (deterministic) sense, it is not a priorily known whether $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$ exists up to time $N^\nu$. Even in the $H^1$ subcritical case where $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$ exists for all time, Theorem \ref{main2} demonstrates the highly nontrivial fact that there is no significant energy shift (such as a cascade) in $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$, (almost) until this very long time $T=N^{(p-1)(s-s_{pr})}$.

In comparison, for deterministic data, say when $g_k(\omega)$ in (\ref{data1}) are replaced by $1$, one can describe the asymptotic behavior of $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$ only up to time\footnote{In fact there is energy shift in $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$ at time $N^{(p-1)(s-s_{cr})}$, dictated by the \emph{continuous resonance} (CR) equation; see \cite{BGHS0,FGH}. Note that, the approximation leading to the CR equation does not work in our case as randomization destroys the differentiability in rescaled Fourier space; in fact the solution $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$ in Theorem \ref{main2} has no energy shift at this time. It is currently unknown whether the solution $u_{\mathrm{ho}}$ in Theorem \ref{main2}, or the corresponding ensemble average, satisfies some effective equation at time $N^{(p-1)(s-s_{pr})}$.} $O(N^{(p-1)(s-s_{cr})})$ provided $s>s_{cr}$; see \cite{BGHS0,FGH} for the $p=3$ case. Therefore, the randomization (\ref{data1}) effectively \emph{extends the time of perturbative regime} for the given homogeneous initial data. In essence, this is the same as Theorem \ref{main}, where we keep the time of perturbative regime constant (namely $1$), and randomization allows us to increase the size of initial data at a given frequency (equivalent to reducing regularity).

\label{tensornorms} Let $A$ be a finite index set, we will denote $k_A=(k_j:j\in A)$. A \emph{tensor} $h=h_{k_A}$ is a function $(\mathbb{Z}^d)^A\to \mathbb{C}$, with $k_A$ being the input variables. The \emph{support} of $h$ is the set of $k_A$ such that $h_{k_A}\neq 0$. These tensors are usually random (i.e. depend on $\omega$ which belongs to the ambient probability space $\Theta$, though we may omit this dependence), hence the name \emph{random tensors}.

A \emph{partition} of $A$ is a pair of sets $(B,C)$ such that $B\cup C=A$ and $B\cap C=\varnothing$. For such $(B,C)$ define the norm $\|\cdot\|_{k_B\to k_C}$ by
 \[\|h\|_{k_B\to k_C}^2=\sup\bigg\{\sum_{k_C}\bigg|\sum_{k_B}h_{k_A}\cdot z_{k_B}\bigg|^2:\sum_{k_B}|z_{k_B}|^2=1\bigg\}.\]By duality we have that 
 \begin{equation}\label{duality}\|h\|_{k_B\to k_C}=\sup\bigg\{\bigg|\sum_{k_B,k_C}h_{k_A}\cdot z_{k_B}\cdot y_{k_C}\bigg|:\sum_{k_B}|z_{k_B}|^2=\sum_{k_C}|y_{k_C}|^2=1\bigg\},
 \end{equation} hence $\|h\|_{k_B\to k_C}=\|h\|_{k_C\to k_B}=\|\overline{h}\|_{k_B\to k_C}$. If $B=\varnothing$ or $C=\varnothing$ we get the norm $\|\cdot\|_{k_A}$ defined by
 \[\|h\|_{k_A}^2=\sum_{k_A}|h_{k_A}|^2.\] Note that trivially $\|h\|_{k_B\to k_C}\leq \|h\|_{k_A}$.
 
 Finally, we define a \emph{subpartition} to be a pair $(B,C)$ such that $B\cup C\subset A$ and $B\cap C=\varnothing$. In such case let $E=A\backslash (B\cup C)$, then $(B,C)$ is a partition of $A\backslash E$ so we can define
 \begin{equation}\label{tensornorms:sup}
  \|h\|_{k_B\to k_C}=\sup_{k_E}\|h_{(k_E,\cdot)}\|_{k_B\to k_C}.
   \end{equation}

The support of h is the set of k_A such that h_k_Aneq 0. These tensors are usually random (i.e. depend on omega which belongs to the ambient probability space Theta, though we may omit this dependence), hence the name random tensors. A partition of A is a pair of sets (B,C) such that Bcup C=A and Bcap C=varnothing. For such (B,C) define the norm \|cdot\|_k_Bto k_C by \[\|h\|_k_Bto k_C^2=supbigg\sum_k_Cbigg|sum_k_Bh_k_Acdot z_k_Bbigg|^2:sum_k_B|z_k_B|^2=1bigg\.\]By duality we have that \|h\|_k_Bto k_C=supbigg\bigg|sum_k_B,k_Ch_k_Acdot z_k_Bcdot y_k_Cbigg|:sum_k_B|z_k_B|^2=sum_k_C|y_k_C|^2=1bigg\, hence \|h\|_k_Bto k_C=\|h\|_k_Cto k_B=\|overlineh\|_k_Bto k_C. If B=varnothing or C=varnothing we get the norm \|cdot\|_k_A defined by \[\|h\|_k_A^2=sum_k_A|h_k_A|^2.\] Note that trivially \|h\|_k_Bto k_Cleq \|h\|_k_A. Finally, we define a subpartition to be a pair (B,C) such that Bcup Csubset A and Bcap C=varnothing. In such case let E=Abackslash (Bcup C), then (B,C) is a partition of Abackslash E so we can define \|h\|_k_Bto k_C=sup_k_E\|h_(k_E,cdot)\|_k_Bto k_C.

nodes.name: Plants
nodes.statement: A plant S consists of the following objects: item Three disjoint finite sets L (called the tree), V (called the blossom set), and Y (called the memory set); elements of L, V and Y are called leaves, blossoms and pasts, and are denoted by l, f and p. An arbitrary element of LcupVcupY is denoted by n. item A collection of pairwise disjoint 2-element subsets of L, which we refer to as pairings; the set of paired leaves is denoted by P, and the set of unpaired leaves is denoted by U:=LbackslashP. item A dyadic number N=N(S) (called the frequency of S), a sign zeta_nin\pm\ for each ninLcupV (note that signs are not defined for pasts), and a dyadic frequency N_n for each ninLcupVcupY. We require that N_l'=N_l and zeta_l'=-zeta_l for any pairing (l,l') in L; that N_nleq N for ninLcupY; and that N_fleq N/2 for finV. We will denote a plant by S=(L,V,Y), and define |S|=|L|+|V|+|Y| to be the size of the plant. Two plants will be identified if there is a bijection between them that preserves all these objects. We say a plant S is regular if N_ngeq N^delta for any ninLcupVcupY, and plain if V=varnothing and sum_linLzeta_l=1 (so in particular |L| is odd). We also define the mini plant S_N^zeta, where zetain\pm\, to be the plant where V=Y=varnothing, L has only one element l with sign zeta and frequency N, and N(S)=N. This is regular, and is plain if zeta=+. Finally we define the conjugate of a plant S to be overlineS, which is the same as S except that the signs of all elements in overlineS are the opposite to the signs in S.
nodes.raw_latex:
\label{defstr} A \emph{plant} $\mathcal{S}$ consists of the following objects:
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item Three disjoint finite sets $\mathcal{L}$ (called the \emph{tree}), $\mathcal{V}$ (called the \emph{blossom set}), and $\mathcal{Y}$ (called the \emph{memory set}); elements of $\mathcal{L}$, $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$ are called \emph{leaves}, \emph{blossoms} and \emph{pasts}, and are denoted by $\mathfrak{l}$, $\mathfrak{f}$ and $\mathfrak{p}$. An arbitrary element of $\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{V}\cup\mathcal{Y}$ is denoted by $\mathfrak{n}$.
 \item A collection of pairwise disjoint $2$-element subsets of $\mathcal{L}$, which we refer to as \emph{pairings}; the set of paired leaves is denoted by $\mathcal{P}$, and the set of unpaired leaves is denoted by $\mathcal{U}:=\mathcal{L}\backslash\mathcal{P}$.
 \item A dyadic number $N=N(\mathcal{S})$ (called the \emph{frequency} of $\mathcal{S}$), a \emph{sign} $\zeta_{\mathfrak{n}}\in\{\pm\}$ for each $\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{V}$ (note that signs are not defined for pasts),  and a dyadic \emph{frequency} $N_{\mathfrak{n}}$ for each $\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{V}\cup\mathcal{Y}$. We require that $N_{\mathfrak{l}'}=N_{\mathfrak{l}}$ and $\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}'}=-\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}$ for any pairing $(\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}')$ in $\mathcal{L}$; that $N_{\mathfrak{n}}\leq N$ for $\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{Y}$; and that $ N_{\mathfrak{f}}\leq N/2$ for $\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}$.
 \end{enumerate} 
 
We will denote a plant by $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{V},\mathcal{Y})$, and define $|\mathcal{S}|=|\mathcal{L}|+|\mathcal{V}|+|\mathcal{Y}|$ to be the \emph{size} of the plant. Two plants will be identified if there is a bijection between them that preserves all these objects. We say a plant $\mathcal{S}$ is \emph{regular} if $N_{\mathfrak{n}}\geq N^\delta$ for any $\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{L}\cup\mathcal{V}\cup\mathcal{Y}$, and \emph{plain} if $\mathcal{V}=\varnothing$ and $\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}=1$ (so in particular $|\mathcal{L}|$ is odd). We also define the \emph{mini plant} $\mathcal{S}_N^\zeta$, where $\zeta\in\{\pm\}$, to be the plant where $\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{Y}=\varnothing$, $\mathcal{L}$ has only one element $\mathfrak{l}$ with sign $\zeta $ and frequency $N$, and $N(\mathcal{S})=N$. This is regular, and is plain if $\zeta=+$. Finally we define the \emph{conjugate} of a plant $\mathcal{S}$ to be $\overline{\mathcal{S}}$, which is the same as $\mathcal{S}$ except that the signs of all elements in $\overline{\mathcal{S}}$ are the opposite to the signs in $\mathcal{S}$.
nodes.clean_text: A plant S consists of the following objects: item Three disjoint finite sets L (called the tree), V (called the blossom set), and Y (called the memory set); elements of L, V and Y are called leaves, blossoms and pasts, and are denoted by l, f and p. An arbitrary element of LcupVcupY is denoted by n. item A collection of pairwise disjoint 2-element subsets of L, which we refer to as pairings; the set of paired leaves is denoted by P, and the set of unpaired leaves is denoted by U:=LbackslashP. item A dyadic number N=N(S) (called the frequency of S), a sign zeta_nin\pm\ for each ninLcupV (note that signs are not defined for pasts), and a dyadic frequency N_n for each ninLcupVcupY. We require that N_l'=N_l and zeta_l'=-zeta_l for any pairing (l,l') in L; that N_nleq N for ninLcupY; and that N_fleq N/2 for finV. We will denote a plant by S=(L,V,Y), and define |S|=|L|+|V|+|Y| to be the size of the plant. Two plants will be identified if there is a bijection between them that preserves all these objects. We say a plant S is regular if N_ngeq N^delta for any ninLcupVcupY, and plain if V=varnothing and sum_linLzeta_l=1 (so in particular |L| is odd). We also define the mini plant S_N^zeta, where zetain\pm\, to be the plant where V=Y=varnothing, L has only one element l with sign zeta and frequency N, and N(S)=N. This is regular, and is plain if zeta=+. Finally we define the conjugate of a plant S to be overlineS, which is the same as S except that the signs of all elements in overlineS are the opposite to the signs in S.

nodes.statement: Note that the sets U,\,L,\,V etc. are associated with a plant S. We will keep this correspondence throughout; for example whenever there is a plant S_j in some context, the set U_j will always be the one coming from S_j. We may encounter sets U_j that do not come from any plant; in such case there will simply be no plant called S_j that appears in the same context.

\label{deftensor} Given a plant $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{V},\mathcal{Y})$, let $\mathcal{U}$ be as in Definition \ref{defstr}. We say a tensor\footnote{In this tensor $k_{\mathcal{V}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$ appear as parameters. Note also that the definition does \emph{not} involve $\mathcal{P}$ or $\mathcal{Y}$.} $h=h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})$ is \emph{an $\mathcal{S}$-tensor}, if $k$ and each $k_{\mathfrak{n}}\,(\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{V})$ are vectors in $\mathbb{Z}^d$, and in the support of $h$ we have that 
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item $\langle k\rangle\leq N$, $\langle k_{\mathfrak{f}}\rangle\leq N_{\mathfrak{f}}$ and $|\lambda_{\mathfrak{f}}|\leq 2N^{\kappa^2}$ for each $\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}$, and $N_{\mathfrak{l}}/2<\langle k_{\mathfrak{l}}\rangle\leq N_{\mathfrak{l}}$ for each $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}$;
 \item there is no pairing in $k_{\mathcal{U}}$, i.e. if $\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'\in\mathcal{U}$ and $\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}'}=-\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}$ then $k_{\mathfrak{l}'}\neq k_{\mathfrak{l}}$.
 \end{enumerate} Here $h$ may depend on other parameters like $t$, in which case we may write $h=h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}(t,k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})$.
  
 Suppose we have defined functions $f_{N'}=(f_{N'})_{k'}$ for any $N'$, and $z_{N'}=(z_{N'})_k(t)$ for any $N'<N$. Define $\Psi_k=\Psi_k[\mathcal{S},h]$ by

 \end{equation} which is an expression determined by the tensor $h$. Note also that an $\mathcal{S}$ tensor $h$ is also an $\overline{\mathcal{S}}$ tensor, and $\overline{\Psi_k[\mathcal{S},h]}=\Psi_k[\overline{\mathcal{S}},\overline{h}]$.

nodes.name: Trimming
nodes.statement: Given a plant S=(L,V,Y) and Rgeq 1, we can trim S at frequency R to get S'=(L',V',Y'), such that L'=\linL:N_lgeq R\ and (V',Y') are defined in the same way. The other objects (i.e. the frequency of S', the signs and frequencies of elements, and the pairings in L') are inherited from S. Obviously, S' is regular if either S is regular or Rgeq N^delta. Now suppose we have defined functions f_N'=(f_N')_k' for any N', and z_N'=(z_N')_k(t) for any N'<R. Then, given an S-tensor h=h_kk_U (k_V,lambda_V), we can trim it at frequency R to get an S'-tensor h'=(h')_kk_U'(k_V',lambda_V'), which is defined by (h')_kk_U'(k_V',lambda_V')=sum_k_UbackslashU'sum_k_VbackslashV'intdlambda_VbackslashV'cdot h_kk_U(k_V,lambda_V)cdotprod_linUbackslashU'(f_N_l)_k_l^zeta_lprod_finVbackslashV'(widehatz_N_f)_k_f^zeta_f(lambda_f). We shall write the above definitions as S'=mathttTrim(S,R) and h'=mathttTrim(h,R). Note that the definition of h' actually depends on the choices of (f_N') and (z_N')_N'<R, but in practice these will be uniquely fixed whenever we apply mathttTrim functions, so we will omit them from the list of parameters. If N_n<R for all ninUcupV then U'=V'=varnothing, and h'=(h')_k is just the Psi_k defined in ().

\label{deftrim} Given a plant $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{L},\mathcal{V},\mathcal{Y})$ and $R\geq 1$, we can \emph{trim $\mathcal{S}$ at frequency $R$} to get $\mathcal{S}'=(\mathcal{L}',\mathcal{V}',\mathcal{Y}')$, such that $\mathcal{L}'=\{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}:N_{\mathfrak{l}}\geq R\}$ and $(\mathcal{V}',\mathcal{Y}')$ are defined in the same way. The other objects (i.e. the frequency of $\mathcal{S}'$, the signs and frequencies of elements, and the pairings in $\mathcal{L}'$) are inherited from $\mathcal{S}$. Obviously, $\mathcal{S}'$ is regular if either $\mathcal{S}$ is regular or $R\geq N^\delta$.
 
 Now suppose we have defined functions $f_{N'}=(f_{N'})_{k'}$ for any $N'$, and $z_{N'}=(z_{N'})_k(t)$ for any $N'<R$. Then, given an $\mathcal{S}$-tensor $h=h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}} }(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})$, we can \emph{trim it at frequency $R$} to get an $\mathcal{S}'$-tensor $h'=(h')_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}(k_{\mathcal{V}'},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}'})$, which is defined by
 \begin{equation}\label{trim1}(h')_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}(k_{\mathcal{V}'},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}'})=\sum_{k_{\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'}}\sum_{k_{\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}}\int\mathrm{d}\lambda_{\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}\cdot h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'}(f_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}})_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}^{\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}}\prod_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}(\widehat{z_{N_{\mathfrak{f}}}})_{k_{\mathfrak{f}}}^{\zeta_{\mathfrak{f}}}(\lambda_{\mathfrak{f}}).
 \end{equation} We shall write the above definitions as $\mathcal{S}'=\mathtt{Trim}(\mathcal{S},R)$ and $h'=\mathtt{Trim}(h,R)$. Note that the definition of $h'$ actually depends on the choices of $(f_{N'})$ and $(z_{N'})_{N'<R}$, but in practice these will be uniquely fixed whenever we apply $\mathtt{Trim}$ functions, so we will omit them from the list of parameters. If $N_{\mathfrak{n}}<R$ for all $\mathfrak{n}\in\mathcal{U}\cup\mathcal{V}$ then $\mathcal{U}'=\mathcal{V}'=\varnothing$, and $h'=(h')_k$ is just the $\Psi_k$ defined in (\ref{defpsi}).

nodes.name: Merging
nodes.statement: First, for any finite set A with a sign for each element, we will fix a maximal collection of pairwise disjoint two-element subsets of A, such that each such subset contains two elements of opposite sign (i.e. pairings). Let P(A) be this collection, and Q(A) be the union of the two-element subsets in P(A). Now let 3leq qleq p be odd and 0leq rleq q. Given dyadic numbers N and N_j and signs zeta_jin\pm\ for 1leq jleq q, so that N_jleq N for 1leq jleq r and N_jleq N/2 for r+1leq jleq q, and sum_j=1^qzeta_j=1, denote the collection of these parameters by B. Given pairwise disjoint plants S_j=(L_j,V_j,Y_j) with frequency N_j for 1leq jleq r, let U_j etc. be as in Definition . Let L:=L_1cupcdots cupL_r andfootnoteIf necessary we may replace the unions cup by the disjoint unions sqcup to avoid repetition of elements. V:=V_1cupcdotscupV_rcup\r+1,cdots,q\, and for each ninL_jcupV_j let the (new) sign of n be zeta_n^*=zeta_jzeta_n, where zeta_n is the sign of n in S_j. Let O=\A_1,cdots,A_m\ be an arbitrary collection of disjoint subsets of W:=U_1cupcdotscupU_r, such that: item each A_i contains two elements of opposite zeta_l^* sign, but does not contain two elements of opposite zeta_l^* sign that belongs to the same U_j; item the frequencies of linA_i are the same for each 1leq ileq m. For each possible O, let P:=P(A_1)cupcdotscupP(A_m) and Q:=Q(A_1)cupcdotscupQ(A_m) with P(cdot) and Q(cdot) defined as above. We then merge S_j\,(1leq jleq r) via B and O, to get a plant S=(L,V,Y) as follows. First N(S)=N, L and V are as above, and the set of pairings in L is the union of the sets of pairings in each L_j, together with P (the new pairings; in particular we have U=WbackslashQ). Second, the sign and frequency of j are given by zeta_j and N_j for r+1leq jleq q, and the sign and frequency of any ninL_jcupV_j\,(1leq jleq r) is given by zeta_n^* and the frequency of n in S_j. Finally, Y=Y_1cupcdotscupY_rcup\0\, with N_0 given by the second maximum of all the N_j\,(1leq jleq q); for any pinY_j\,(1leq jleq r) the frequency of p in S equals the frequency of p in S_j. Now suppose we have defined a tensor h=h_kk_1cdots k_q(lambda_r+1,cdots,lambda_q), where k,k_1,cdots ,k_q are input variables and lambda_r+1,cdots,lambda_q are parameters; assume in the support of h that langle krangleleq N and langle k_jrangleleq N_j for 1leq jleq q, and that |lambda_j|leq 2N^kappa^2 for r+1leq jleq q. Then, given S_j-tensors h^(j)=h_k_jk_U_j^(j)(k_V_j,lambda_V_j), where 1leq jleq r, we shall merge these h^(j) via h, B and O, to form a new tensor H=H_kk_U(k_V,lambda_V), namely H_kk_U(k_V,lambda_V)=prod_l,l'^(1)1_k_l=k_l'prod_l,l'^(2)1_k_lneq k_l'cdotsum_(k_1,cdots,k_r)h_kk_1cdots k_q(lambda_r+1,cdots,lambda_q)\\timessum_k_Q^(3)prod_linQDelta_N_lgamma_k_lprod_j=1^rbig[h_k_jk_U_j^(j)(k_V_j,lambda_V_j)big]^zeta_j. In the above expression, the product prod_l,l'^(1) is taken over all leaves l,l'inU such that they belong to the same A_i (in particular zeta_l'^*=zeta_l^*), the product prod_l,l'^(2) is taken over all leaves l,l'in U such thatfootnoteHere we may also require N_l=N_l'; whether we do so will not affect the result of this product. zeta_l'^*=-zeta_l^* (so they do not belong to the same A_i), and the summation sum_k_Q^(3) is taken over all possible k_Q (with Q defined above) such that for each i, all the k_l for linQcapA_i are equal, and they equal k_l' for l'inUcapA_i (if such l' exists). We can verify that H is an S-tensor. We shall write the above definitions as S=mathttMerge(S_1,cdots,S_r,B,O), H=mathttMerge(h^(1),cdots,h^(r),h,B,O).

nodes.statement: Assume we have fixed the choices of f_N' and z_N' as in Definitions and , and h=h_kk_1cdots k_q(lambda_r+1,cdots,lambda_q), B, S_j and S_j-tensors h^(j) for 1leq jleq r as in Definition . In applying the mathttMerge function below we will omit the parameters h and B. Then the following statements hold: (1) Recall the definition of Psi_k=Psi_k[cdot,cdot] as in (). Then for any R we have Psi_k[S_j,h^(j)]=Psi_k[mathttTrim(S_j,R),mathttTrim(h^(j),R)]. Similarly, trimming at frequency R_1 and then R_2 is equivalent to trimming once at max(R_1,R_2). (2) Let Psi_k_j^(j)=Psi_k_j[S_j,h^(j)] be defined as in () from the S_j-tensor h^(j) for 1leq jleq r. Then the quantity Phi_k:=sum_(k_1,cdots,k_q)intdlambda_r+1cdotsdlambda_qcdot h_kk_1cdots k_q(lambda_r+1,cdots,lambda_q)cdotprod_j=1^r(Psi_k_j^(j))^zeta_jprod_j=r+1^q(widehatz_N_j)_k_j^zeta_j(lambda_j) can be written as a linear combinationfootnoteHere and below the phrase ``linear combination'' will refer to a linear combination with a fixed number of terms and fixed constant coefficients. of Psi_k=Psi_k[S,H] (for different choices of O as in Definition ), where \[S=mathttMerge(S_1,cdots,S_r,O), H=mathttMerge(h^(1),cdots,h^(r),O).\] (3) Let S_j'=(L_j',V_j',Y_j')=mathttTrim(S_j,N^delta) and (h^(j))'=mathttTrim(h^(j),N^delta) for 1leq jleq r. Then for the plant S=mathttTrim(mathttMerge(mathttTrim(S_1,N^delta),cdots,mathttTrim(S_r,N^delta),O),N^delta) where O is as in Definition , we have |S|>|S_j|. We may assume $p_1=p$, since if $p_1<p$ we can add some elements to the sets $B_u$ and reduce to the $p_1=p$ case. We will prove (\ref{basiccounting1}) by induction. Suppose (\ref{basiccounting1}) is true for $p-2$, we will prove it for $p$. For simplicity we define
 \[w_{i_u(y)}:=\sum_{z=1}^y\zeta_{i_u(z)}k_{i_u(z)},\quad 1\leq u\leq t,\,1\leq y\leq b_u.\]
 
 Since $p$ is odd, at least one of $|B_u|$ (say $|B_1|$) must be odd. If $|B_1|=1$ then the value of $k_{i_1(1)}$ is fixed, so we only need to count the vector $k_{A\backslash B_1}$. If $|B_2|=1$ also then we may reduce to counting $k_{A\backslash (B_1\cup B_2)}$ and apply the induction hypothesis; otherwise $|B_2|\geq 2$ and we may add an element to $B_2$ at no cost and reduce to the case $|B_2|\geq 3$. Therefore in any case we may assume some $|B_j|\geq 3$, say $|B_1|=b_1\geq 3$.
 
Let $(i_1(b_1),i_1(b_1-1),i_1(b_1-2))=(n,n',n'')$. Since by (\ref{basicset}), each $w_{i_u(y)}$ belongs to a ball of radius $M_{i_u(y)}$, and $k_{i_u(y)}=\pm w_{i_u(y)}\pm w_{i_u(y-1)}$ for some choices of $\pm$ (same below), the number of choices for the vector $k_{B_1\backslash\{n,n',n''\}}$ is at most\[M_{i_1(1)}^d\cdots M_{i_1(b_1-3)}^d=(M_{n'}M_{n''})^{-d}\prod_{j\in B_1}M_j^d,\] noticing that $M_n=1$. Similarly for $2\leq u\leq t$, the number of choices for the vector $k_{B_u}$ is at most $\prod_{j\in B_u}M_j^d$. Once $k_{A\backslash\{n,n',n''\}}$ is fixed, $k_{n''}=\pm w_{n''}\pm w_{i_1(b_1-3)}$ belongs to a ball of radius $M_{n''}$, and $k_n=\pm w_n\pm w_{n'}$ belongs to a ball of radius $M_{n'}$. Then the number of choices for $(k_n,k_{n'},k_{n''})$ can be bounded by $(M_{n'}M_{n''})^{d-1+\theta}$ by Lemma \ref{cubic}, thus
\begin{equation}\label{interpolate1}\#S\lesssim (M_{n'}M_{n''})^{d-1+\theta}\prod_{j\in A\backslash\{n,n',n''\}}M_j^d.\end{equation} Note that this also settles the base case $p=3$.

On the other hand, for $p\geq 5$, since $M_n=1$, by (\ref{basicset}) we know that $k_n=\pm w_{n}\pm w_{n'}$ belongs to a ball of radius $M_{n'}$, and when $k_n$ is fixed, $k_{n'}=\pm w_n\pm k_n\pm w_{n''}$ belongs to a ball of radius $M_{n''}$. Thus the number of choices for $(k_n,k_{n'})$ is at most $(M_{n'}M_{n''})^d$. When $(k_n,k_{n'})$ is fixed, we only need to count the vectors $k_{A\backslash\{n,n'\}}$. Now $w_{i_1(y)}$ belongs to a ball of radius $M_{i_1(y)}$ if $y\leq b_1-3$, and to a ball of radius $1$ if $y=b_1-2$, so by the induction hypothesis we conclude that
\begin{equation}\label{interpolate2}\#S\lesssim (M_{n'}M_{n''})^{d}\prod_{j\in A\backslash\{n,n',n''\}}M_j^{d-\frac{2}{p-3}+\theta}.\end{equation} Interpolating (\ref{interpolate1}) and (\ref{interpolate2}) we get
\[\#S\lesssim\prod_{j\in A\backslash\{n\}}M_j^{d-\frac{2}{p-1}+\theta},\] which is just (\ref{basiccounting1}).

\label{mainprop} Given a dyadic $M$, consider the following set of statements (viewed as an event for $\omega$), which we shall refer to as $\mathtt{Local}(M)$ below: 

(1) For any plain regular plant $\mathcal{S}=(\mathcal{L},\varnothing,\mathcal{Y})$ with $N(\mathcal{S})=N< M$ and $|\mathcal{S}|\leq D$, we have that
\begin{equation}\label{support01} h^{(\mathcal{S},0)}=h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}^{(\mathcal{S},0)}(t)\mathrm{\ is\ supported\ in\ the\ set\ where\ }k=\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}.
\end{equation}For any $\Gamma\in\mathbb{Z}$, let $h^{(\mathcal{S},0,\Gamma)}$ be the restriction of $h^{(\mathcal{S},0)}$ to the set where
 \begin{equation}\label{support02} |k|^2-\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}|k_{\mathfrak{l}}|^2=\Gamma,
 \end{equation} obtained by multiplying by the indicator function of this set. Let $(B,C)$ be a subpartition of $\mathcal{U}$ and let $E=\mathcal{U}\backslash(B\cup C)$. Then we have
 \begin{equation}\label{estimate01}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\langle \lambda\rangle^{2b}\bigg(\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathbb{Z}}\|\widehat{h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}^{(\mathcal{S},0,\Gamma)}}(\lambda)\|_{kk_B\to k_C}\bigg)^2\,\mathrm{d}\lambda\leq\bigg(\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in B\cup C}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{\beta_1}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{P}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-8\varepsilon}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in E}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{4\varepsilon}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\in\mathcal{Y}}N_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-\delta^3}\cdot\mathcal{X}_0\mathcal{X}_1\bigg)^2,
 \end{equation} with the quantities
 \begin{equation}\label{estimate02}\mathcal{X}_0=\left\{
  \begin{aligned}&\big(\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in C}N_{\mathfrak{l}}\big)^{-\beta_1},&&\mathrm{if\ }C\neq\varnothing;\\
    & \big(\min_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}\big)^{\frac{d}{2}-\beta_1},&&\mathrm{if\ }C=E=\varnothing;\\
   & N^{-\varepsilon\delta},&&\mathrm{if\ }B=C=\varnothing;\\
    &1,&&\mathrm{otherwise},
 \end{aligned}
 \right.\qquad\mathcal{X}_1=\left\{
 \begin{aligned}&1,&{\rm{if }}\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in \mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}&\geq (10^3dp)^{-|\mathcal{L}|}N;\\
&N^{-4\varepsilon},&{\rm{if }}\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in \mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}&< (10^3dp)^{-|\mathcal{L}|}N.
 \end{aligned}
 \right.
 \end{equation}

(1) By definition we have
\begin{equation}\label{trimexpand}
\begin{split} h'=h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}'(k_{\mathcal{V}'},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}'})&=\sum_{k_{\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}}\int\mathrm{d}\lambda_{\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}\cdot \widetilde{h}_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})\prod_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}(\widehat{z_{N_{\mathfrak{f}}}})_{k_{\mathfrak{f}}}^{\zeta_{\mathfrak{f}}}(\lambda_{\mathfrak{f}}),\\
\widetilde{h}_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})&:=\sum_{k_{\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'}}h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'}(f_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}})_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}^{\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}}.
\end{split}\end{equation} By Cauchy-Schwartz we have 
\begin{equation}\label{blostep0}\|h'\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}'}^{-b_0}[\cdots]}\lesssim\|\widetilde{h}\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]}\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'}\|z_{N_{\mathfrak{f}}}\|_{X^{b_0}}\lesssim \|\widetilde{h}\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]}\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'} N_{\mathfrak{f}}^{-D_1},\end{equation} where $[\cdots]$ represents any $kk_{B'}\to k_{C'}$ or $kk_{B'}$ or weighted norm as in (\ref{trim-bd1})--(\ref{trim-bd3}).

It thus suffices to bound the corresponding norms for $\widetilde{h}$. Note that if we \emph{fix the values of} $k_{\mathcal{V}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$, the tensor $\widetilde{h}_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})$ can be estimated $\tau^{-1}M$-certainly, using Proposition \ref{gausscont}; in order to transform this to a bound for the $X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]$ norms, we need to make this bound \emph{uniform in all choices of $k_{\mathcal{V}}$ and $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$}. There is no problem in doing so for $k_{\mathcal{V}}$ since\footnote{The same applies to the $k_E$ variables when measuring $kk_B\to k_C$ norms, where $E=\mathcal{U}\backslash(B\cup C)$.} the number of choices for $k_{\mathcal{V}}$ is at most $M^{\kappa}$. To deal with $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$, we will employ the following argument, which will be referred to as the \emph{meshing argument} (see the proof of Lemma 4.2 in \cite{DNY}), and will be used frequently in the proofs below. First note that $|\lambda_{\mathfrak{f}}|\lesssim N^{\kappa^2}$ for each $\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}$, then we divide the big box $\{\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}:|\lambda_{\mathfrak{f}}|\lesssim N^{\kappa^2},\forall\,\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}\}$ into small boxes $\mathfrak{B}$ of size $\nu:=\exp(-(\log N)^6)$. Now by taking averages on these small boxes and using Poincar\'{e} inequality, there exists a tensor $h_{\mathrm{avg}}=(h_{\mathrm{avg}})_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})$ such that $h_{\mathrm{avg}}$ satisfies the same measurability condition as $h$, that $h_{\mathrm{avg}}$ is supported in the big box and constant when $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$ moves within each small box (and other parameters are fixed), and that
\begin{equation}\label{approx}\|h-h_{\mathrm{avg}}\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[kk_{\mathcal{U}}]}\lesssim\nu\cdot(\|h\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[kk_{\mathcal{U}}]}+\|\partial_{\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}}h\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[kk_{\mathcal{U}}]}).\end{equation} Let $\widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{avg}}$ be defined from $h_{\mathrm{avg}}$, in the same way as $\widetilde{h}$ is defined from $h$, then for \emph{fixed values of} $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$, the tensor $(\widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{avg}})_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}'}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})$ can be estimated $\tau^{-1}M$-certainly, using Proposition \ref{gausscont}, in the same way that $\widetilde{h}$ is bounded in terms of $h$. Since $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$ has at most $\exp(\kappa(\log N)^6)$ different choices in studying $h_{\mathrm{avg}}$, and $N\leq M$, we know that the estimate for $\widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{avg}}$ is \emph{uniform in all choices of} $\lambda_{\mathcal{V}}$, after removing an exceptional set whose probability is still $\leq C_\theta e^{-(\tau^{-1}M)^\theta}$. This gives the $X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]$ norm bounds for $\widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{avg}}$; but by (\ref{trim-bd4}), (\ref{approx}) and our choice for $\nu$, the $X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]$ norm of the difference $\widetilde{h}-\widetilde{h}_{\mathrm{avg}}$ is negligible, so we get the desired $X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]$ norm bounds for $\widetilde{h}$.

Armed with the meshing argument, we can now apply Proposition \ref{gausscont} to control the $X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[\cdots]$ norms of $\widetilde{h}$. Given any subpartition $(B',C')$ of $\mathcal{U}'$, $C'\neq\varnothing$, let $E=E'=\mathcal{U}'\backslash(B'\cup C')$; since $h$ is $\mathcal{B}_{N^{[\delta]}}$ measurable and $N_{\mathfrak{l}}>N^{[\delta]}$ for all $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}$, we can apply Proposition \ref{gausscont} (note that $(f_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}})_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}=\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}\cdot\eta_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}(\omega)$, where $\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}$ can be replaced by $\tau^{-\theta}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+\theta}$ due to (\ref{constants}) and Lemma \ref{adjustment}) to get
\[\|\widetilde{h}_{kk_{\mathcal{U}'}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[kk_{B'}\to k_{C'}]}\lesssim\tau^{-\theta}M^\theta\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+\theta}\cdot\sup_{(F,G)}\|h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}(k_{\mathcal{V}},\lambda_{\mathcal{V}})\|_{X_{\mathcal{V}}^{-b_0}[kk_{B}\to k_{C}]},\] where $(F,G)$ is any partition of $\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'$, and $B=B'\cup F$, $C=C'\cup G$. The conclusion about the $X_{\mathcal{V}'}^{-b_0}[kk_{B'}\to k_{C'}]$ norms then follows by combining (\ref{trim-bd1}) and (\ref{blostep0}), and noticing that $\mathcal{P}'\subset\mathcal{P}$, $\mathcal{Y}'\subset\mathcal{Y}$, and $\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in C'}N_{\mathfrak{l}}=\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in C}N_{\mathfrak{l}}$. When $C'=\varnothing$, the proofs for the $X_{\mathcal{V}'}^b[kk_{B'}]$ norms are completely analogous (simply choose $G=\varnothing$ so $C=\varnothing$), and so is the weighted norm bound, where for the latter we notice that
\[1+\frac{1}{\max(N^{2\delta},R)}\bigg|k-\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}'}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}-\ell'\bigg|\lesssim 1+\frac{1}{N^{2\delta}}\bigg|k-\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}-\ell\bigg|\] with $\ell'=\sum_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}'}\zeta_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{f}}$ and $\ell=\sum_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}}\zeta_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{f}}$, since $\langle k_{\mathfrak{f}}\rangle\leq R$ for any $\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}\backslash\mathcal{V}'$ (hence $|\ell-\ell'|\lesssim R$) and $\langle k_{\mathfrak{l}}\rangle\leq R$ for any $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'$.

(2) The proof is similar to (1) but much easier since there is no blossom $\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}$ (hence no meshing argument) involved. Since $|k-\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}'}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}|\lesssim R$ because $k-\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}=0$ and $\langle k_{\mathfrak{l}}\rangle\leq R$ for $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}\backslash\mathcal{U}'$, we know that the weighted norm bound (\ref{trim-bd3}) follows from the unweighted norm bound (\ref{trim-bd2}). For the $kk_{B'}\to k_{C'}$ norms in (\ref{trim-bd1})--(\ref{trim-bd2}), we simply apply Proposition \ref{gausscont}; when $C'\neq\varnothing$ we readily get (\ref{trim-bd1}) with the indicated changes. When $C'=\varnothing$ (and $C=\varnothing$) we make two observations. First, when $E=E'=\varnothing$ there is an extra factor $\mathcal{X}_0$ in (\ref{trim-bd5}), but since $\min_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}\leq R$ due to the assumption $\mathcal{L}\neq\mathcal{L}'$, we have $\mathcal{X}_0\lesssim R^{d/2-\beta_1}$ by definition (\ref{estimate02}), which gives rise to the factor $R^{d/2-\beta_1}$ in the desired estimate. Second, thanks to the different powers between (\ref{trim-bd1})--(\ref{trim-bd3}) and (\ref{trim-bd5}), in the process of using (\ref{trim-bd5}) for $h$ to deduce (\ref{trim-bd1})--(\ref{trim-bd2}) for $h'$, we will be gaining a factor
\[\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in \mathcal{U}\backslash E'}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{\beta_1-\beta}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in E'\cup\mathcal{P}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-4\varepsilon}\leq\big(\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}\big)^{-4\varepsilon},\] which is at most $N^{-4\varepsilon}$ if $\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}\geq (10^3dp)^{-|\mathcal{L}|}N$. If $\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{L}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}< (10^3dp)^{-|\mathcal{L}|}N$ we gain exactly the same $N^{-4\varepsilon}$ from the factor $\mathcal{X}_1$ in (\ref{estimate02}). In any case, this gain will contribute the $N^{-3\varepsilon}$ in the desired estimate, after providing the $N^{-\varepsilon}$ factor for (\ref{trim-bd2}).

The two key ingredients in the proof are Proposition and Proposition . Step 1: first reductions. We start by making an adjustment in notations, just like the one in the proof of Proposition , which will allow us to apply Proposition below. For each pairing (l,l'), where lin U_j and l'inU_j', since in the sum () we are always assuming k_l=k_l', we may combine them into a single element and include this element in both U_j and U_j'. In this way we are changing pairings between different U_j's to intersections of different U_j's, which is the setting of Proposition . Then U will be the set of elements that occurs once in all the U_j's, and Q is the set of elements that occur twice. Next, we will identify all subsets Asubset\2,cdots,p\ such that each and every element in the union of U_j\,(jin A) occurs twice in these sets U_j\,(jin A). We only need to consider minimal subsets A that satisfy this, which will be pairwise disjoint. Let them be A_v\,(1leq vleq s) and B_u\,(1leq uleq t), where for each v, the tensor h^(j) is of type R0 for each jin A_v, while for each u, there is at least one jin B_u such that the tensor h^(j) is of type R0^+ or R1. Let E be the union of all these sets A_v and B_u and D=\2,cdots,p ackslash E; See Figure for an illustration of the above subsets of \2,cdots,p\. We know that U_jsubsetQ for jin E. includegraphics[width=0.65textwidth]graph_62 captionClassification of U_j, jin \2,cdots,p\ Let Rsubset Q be the set of elements that occur twice in the sets U_j (jinD). Then we have H=H_kk_1k_U=sum_(k_A_1,cdots k_A_s,k_B_1,cdots k_B_t)prod_v=1^s H_k_A_v^[v]prod_u=1^tR_k_B_u^[u]cdot H^sg_kk_1k_Ek_U, where H_k_A_v^[v]:=sum_(k_U_j:jin A_v)prod_jin A_vh_k_jk_U_j^(j), R_k_B_u^[u]:=sum_(k_U_j:jin B_u)prod_jin B_uh_k_jk_U_j^(j), H^sg_kk_1k_Ek_U:=sum_(k_D,k_R)h_kk_1cdots k_pcdotprod_jin Dh_k_jk_U_j^(j). By () and Proposition we have \|H\|_kk_Pto k_1k_Qleq prod_q=1^s\|H^[v]\|_k_A_vprod_u=1^t\|R^[u]\|_k_B_ucdot\|H^sg\|_kk_Pto k_1k_Ek_Q, so it suffices to bound the norm \|H^sg\|_kk_Pto k_1k_E k_Q and the other norms \|H^[v]\|_k_A_v and \|R^[u]\|_k_B_u. By (), the tensor H^sg is a semi-product the tensors h and h^(j)\,(jin D) in the sense of () in Proposition , so our strategy is to select these tensors in some particular order and apply Proposition . The selection algorithm is described as follows. Step 2: the selection algorithm for H^sg. First, by our choice of the set D, there will be at least one element in the union of the sets U_j\,(jin D) that appears only once in these sets. Consider such an element l with N_l being the biggest. Denote this l by l_c-1 and the jin D such that l_c-1in U_j by n_c-1, where c-1=|C|-1=|D| and C=Dcup\1\. Next, there will be at least one element in the union of the sets U_j\,(jin Dbackslash
_c-1\) that appears only once in these sets. Consider such an element l=l_c-2 such that N_l is the biggest, and suppose such l_c-2in U_j', where j'in Dbackslash
_c-1\; we shall denote n_c-2=j'. Next there will be at least one element in the union of the sets U_j\,(jin Dbackslash
_c-1,n_c-2\) that appears only once in these sets, and so on. Repeating this process, we can label the elements of D as n_1, n_2, cdots, n_c-1. Notice that by () and () and our selection algorithm, for each 1leq yleq c-1 we must have bigg|sum_z=1^yzeta_n_zk_n_z-m_n_y'bigg|lesssim max((N_*)^3delta, N_l_y):=M_n_y, where m_n_y'inZ^d is some fixed vector, otherwise the product in () will be zero. Let us provide some details to explain (). When y=1, l_1in U_n_1 and N_l_1 is the biggest among all l that appear only once in U_n_1 (here these l's are just all elements lin U_n_1). By (), () and (), setting m_n_1'=zeta_n_1m_n_1, we then have |zeta_n_1k_n_1 - m'_n_1| leq |U_n_1| N_l_1 +(N_*)^3delta, where we understand that m_n_1=0 if h^(n_1) has type R0 (same below), which implies () since |U_n_1|leq D. When y=2, l_2in U_n_2 and N_l_2 is the biggest among all l that appear only once in U_n_1cup U_n_2 (i.e. all linU_n_1Delta U_n_2), then by (), () and (), we have |zeta_n_1k_n_1+zeta_n_2k_n_2-m'_n_2|lesssim max((N_*)^3delta, N_l_2) with m'_n_2=zeta_n_1 m_n_1+zeta_n_2 m_n_2, since the k_l terms for linU_n_1cap U_n_2 always cancel themselves thanks to our assumption about signs of paired elements. For the other y's, () is obtained similarly. The above selection for n_c-1,cdots, n_1 is designed to fit the hypothesis () in Proposition via (). Proposition will be applied to h later in Step 4. Next, we divide these n_y into two classes: first n_c-1 will be class P (or Q) if l_c-1 which belongs to U, is in P (or Q). Next, if l_c-2in U, then n_c-2 will be class P (or Q) if l_c-2 is in P (or Q); if l_c-2inQ, then l_c-2 also belongs to U_j for some previously selected j (here j=n_c-1), then n_c-2 will be same class as j. Then consider l_c-3, and so on. Repeating this process we can assign a class P or Q to each n_y\,(1leq yleq c-1). Now we can apply Proposition by arranging the tensors h and h^(j)\,(jin D) in a particular order (which will correspond to the superscripts in the tensors in Proposition ): first list all the h^(n_y), where n_y has class Q, in the decreasing order for y, then list h, then list all the h^(n_y), where n_y has class P, in the increasing order for y. By applying Proposition to () with (k_A, k_C, k_X, k_Y) = (kk_1k_E k_U, k_D k_R, kk_P, k_1 k_E k_Q) in the above order we then have \|H^sg\|_kk_Pto k_1k_E k_Qlesssim\|h\|_kk_P_0to k_Q_0prod_j\,of\,class\,Q\|h^(j)\|_k_jk_P_jto k_Q_j prod_j\,of\,class\,P\|h^(j)\|_k_Q_jto k_j k_P_j, where (P_0,Q_0) and (P_j,Q_j)\,(jinD) are sets defined according to Proposition , which are explained next. Next we analyze the individual factors on the right hand side of (). (1) For j=n_y of class Q, by Proposition and our algorithm, the set Q_j will consist of all lin U_n_y such that either lin Q, or l belongs to U_n_y' for some y'>y with n_y' of class Q. Furthermore P_j = U_jbackslash Q_j. By the definition of classes, this implies that l_yin Q_j. By () and () we then have \|h^(j)\|_k_jk_P_jto k_Q_jlesssim X_jcdotprod_linU_j N_l^betacdot N_l_y^-betalesssim X_jcdotprod_linU_j N_l^betacdot (N_*)^CdeltaM_n_y^-beta; moreover if h^(j) has type R0 or R0^+, we gain an extra factor namely Z_1,j from (). (2) Similarly, for j=n_y of class P, by Proposition and our algorithm, the set Q_j will consist of all linU_n_y such that either lin P, or l belongs to U_n_y' for some y'>y with n_y' of class P. Now by (), (), and using the duality of the operator norm \|h^(j)\|_k_Q_jto k_jk_P_j=\|h^(j)\|_k_jk_P_jto k_Q_j, we know that () is true (with the gain Z_1,j for types R0 and R0^+) also in this case. Next, as in \emph{Step 2} there will be at least one element in the union of the sets $\mathcal{U}_j\,(j\in A_v\backslash\{\ell_v(a_v)\})$ that appears only once in these sets.

  \begin{equation}\label{cancellation2}\bigg|\sum_{z=1}^y\zeta_{\ell_v(z)}k_{\ell_v(z)}\bigg|\lesssim N_{\mathfrak{l}_y}:=M_{\ell_v(y)},

  \end{equation}
    \begin{equation}\label{actbd3} \|h^{(j)}\|_{k_jk_{P_j}\to k_{Q_j}}\lesssim \mathfrak{X}_j\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in \mathcal{U}_j}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{\beta_1}\cdot (N_{\mathfrak{l}_{a_v}})^{\frac{d}{2}-\beta_1}\cdot\mathcal{Z}_{1,j},\quad  \mathrm{if\ }j=\ell_v(a_v),

\begin{equation}\label{lastbd'}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{Q}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+4\varepsilon+\theta}\cdot\|H\|_{kk_P\to k_1k_Q}\lesssim \prod_{j=2}^{p}\mathfrak{X}_j\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^\beta\cdot (N_*)^{C\delta}(\max_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}_j, 2\leq j\leq p}N_{\mathfrak{l}})^{-4p\varepsilon}\prod_j^{(0,0^+)}\mathcal{Z}_{1,j}.

Otherwise, let $2\leq j\leq p$ be such that $N_j=N_*$, then $N_{\mathfrak{l}}\ll N_j^{\varepsilon^2}$ for all $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}_j$. If $h^{(j)}$ has type $R0$ or $R0^+$, the factor $\mathcal{Z}_{1,j}^{1/2}=N_j^{-2\varepsilon}$ in the other square root  is bounded by $(N_*)^{-C\delta- \varepsilon^3}$. \begin{equation}\label{type2bd2'}

for any partition $(P_j, Q_j)$ of $\mathcal{U}_j$. Then we gain an extra factor $N_j^{-\varepsilon/2}$ (which is less than $(N_*)^{-C\delta- \varepsilon^3}$) by using (\ref{type2bd2'}) instead of (\ref{type2bd2}) in (\ref{actbd1}), (\ref{actbd4}) or (\ref{actbd5}),  and hence (\ref{outputbd}) is proved.

\[\sup_{k_j}\|h^{(j)}\|_{k_{\mathcal{U}_j}}\leq \|h^{(j)}\|_{k_j\to k_{\mathcal{U}_j}}.\] One can check that the power gain coming from using these norms is enough to cancel the summation in $k$, and the rest of the proof goes just like above. nodes.statement: We would like to apply Proposition . The technical difficulty before doing so is two-folded. On the one hand, we must separate the tensor h^(1) from the tensor H defined in (). On the other hand, since there are no over-pairings in the statement of Proposition we must remove these from H. Once we have dealt with this technical difficulty, the heart of the matter lies in implementing Proposition to obtain the desired bounds above. In the proof below we will mainly focus on (). The proof of () will be analogous, and we will only point out the necessary changes in the course of the proof. Moreover, in proving () we will only use the bound () for the tensor h^(1), so () will follow from the same arguments as () once we use () instead of (), in view of () and Klesssim K_1, N_1leq M. The proof will proceed in four steps. In Step 1, we reduce the desired estimates for the tensor H to those for the tensor H^circ defined in () below. In Step 2, we remove and estimate the over-pairings, and reduce the desired estimates for H^circ to those for (H^circ)^dagger defined in (). In Step 3, we first single out h^(1) in (H^circ)^dagger and in turn apply Propositions and , then remove and estimate the over-pairings as in Step 2, to reduce the desired estimates for (H^circ)^dagger to those for H^dagger defined in (). Finally in Step 4, we implement Proposition and conclude the proof. Step 1: pre-processing. Define \[widetildeS=(widetildeL,widetildeV,widetildeY)=mathttMerge(S_1,cdots,S_r,B,O),\]\[widetildeH=widetildeH_kk_widetildeU(k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV)=mathttMerge(h^(1),cdots, h^(r),h,B,O),\] noticing that widetildeV=V_1cupcdotscupV_rcup\r+1,cdots,q\, and define H^circ=(H^circ)_kk_U(k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV)=sum_k_widetildeUbackslashUwidetildeH_kk_widetildeU(k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV)prod_lin widetildeUbackslashU(f_N_l)_k_l^zeta_l^*, then we have \[H_kk_U(k_V,lambda_V)=sum_k_widetildeVbackslashVintdlambda_widetildeVbackslashVcdot(H^circ)_kk_U(k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV)prod_finwidetildeVbackslashV(widehatz_N_f)_k_f^zeta_f^*(lambda_f).\] By the same proof as part (1) of Proposition , for any X_V^-b_0[cdots] norm we have \|H\|_X_V^-b_0[cdots]lesssim\|H^circ\|_X_widetildeV^-b_0[cdots]cdotprod_finwidetildeVbackslashVN_f^-D_1, as well as for the weighted norm in (). Therefore, it suffices to estimate the X_widetildeV^-b_0[cdots] norms (as well as the weighted ones) for H^circ. For each 1leq jleq r, if h^(j) has type 1, we can define X_j^*=X_j^*(k_V_j,lambda_V_j) to be the smallest positive number such that the bounds ()--() are true for this choice of (k_V_j,lambda_V_j) with X_V_j^-b_0 in the norms removed (for example X_V_j^-b_0[k_jk_B_jto k_C_j] replaced by k_jk_B_jto k_C_j), and with X_j replaced by X_j^*(k_V_j,lambda_V_j); for example one of the inequalities satisfied by X_j^*=X_j^*(k_V_j,lambda_V_j), which corresponds to (), would be \|h^(j)\|_k_jk_B_jto k_C_jlesssimX_j^*cdottau^-thetaprod_lin B_jcup C_jN_l^betaprod_linP_jN_l^-4varepsilonprod_lin E_jN_l^8varepsilonprod_pinY_jN_p^-delta^3 prod_f in V_j N_f^dcdot big(max_lin C_jN_lbig)^-beta with C_jneqvarnothing, for fixed (k_V_j,lambda_V_j). If h^(j) has type 0, we simply define X_j^*=X_j. Then we have sum_k_V_jintdlambda_V_jcdotprod_finV_jlangle lambda_frangle^-2b_0cdotX_j^*(k_V_j,lambda_V_j)^2lesssim X_j^2 for type 1 tensors. When (k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV) is fixed, which means (k_V_j,lambda_V_j) are fixed for 1leq jleq r and (k_j,lambda_j) are fixed for r+1leq jleq q, we shall view h=h_kk_1cdots k_r as a tensor depending on (k,k_1,cdots,k_r); for 1leq jleq r we shall view h^(j)=h_k_jk_U_j^(j) as a tensor depending on (k_j,k_U_j). With these reductions, we can view widetildeH=widetildeH_kk_widetildeU as a tensor depending on (k,k_widetildeU) and H^circ=H_kk_U^circ depending on (k,k_U), namely widetildeH_kk_widetildeU=prod_l,l'^(1)1_k_l=k_l'prod_l,l'^(2)1_k_lneq k_l'cdotsum_(k_1,cdots,k_r)h_kk_1cdots k_rsum_k_Q^(3)prod_linQDelta_N_lgamma_k_lprod_j=1^rbig[h_k_jk_U_j^(j)big]^zeta_j, (H^circ)_kk_U=sum_k_widetildeUbackslashUwidetildeH_kk_widetildeUprod_lin widetildeUbackslashU(f_N_l)_k_l^zeta_l^*, where in (), the sum and products are taken in the same way as () when merging the tensors (h^(1),cdots,h^(r)) via (h,B,O). Similarly Q is defined as in Definition . Also note that U =\linwidetildeU:N_lgeq M^delta\. Our goal is to prove that, for fixed values of (k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV) defined in (), the tensor H^circ=H_kk_U^circ satisfies (), () and () tau^-1M-certainly, but with the following three adjustments: (a) we remove the X_V^-b_0 parts in the norms (for example X_V^-b_0[kk_Bto k_C] is replaced by kk_Bto k_C), and multiply the left hand sides by the extra factor prod_j=r+1^q N_j^-d/2; (b) the set V in the factors prod_finVN_f^d on the right hand sides is replaced by V_1cupcdotscupV_r and Y is replaced by widetildeY; and (c) the X_j in the definition () of Y is replaced by X_j^*. For example, the analogue of () with the above adjustments (a)--(c) amounts to showing: sqrtUpsiloncdotprod_j=r+1^q N_j^-d/2\,\|H^circ\|_kk_Bto k_Clesssim&tau^-thetaprod_lin Bcup CN_l^betaprod_linPN_l^-4varepsilonprod_lin EN_l^8varepsilonbig(max_lin CN_lbig)^-beta\\ &times prod_pinwidetildeYN_p^-delta^3\, prod_f in V_1cupcdotscupV_r N_f^d cdotleft( prod_j=1^rX^*_jcdottau^-thetaM^theta(N_*)^-2varepsilon^4right), where prod_j=1^rX^*_jcdottau^-thetaM^theta(N_*)^-2varepsilon^4 is Y in () with replacements of X_j by X_j^*. The corresponding analogues of () and () with the adjustments (a)--(c) are similar. If we can prove () for a fixed choice of (k_widetildeV, lambda_widetildeV) in H^circ, then by applying the meshing argument in the same way as we did in the proof of Proposition , using () and (), we can reduce to the case of at most exp(kappa(log M)^6) choices for (k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV), hence tau^-1M-certainly we may assume that () holds for H_kk_U^circ for all choices of (k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV). Since widetildeV=V_1cupcdotscupV_rcup\r+1,cdots,q\ and the definition of X_widetildeV^-b_0[cdots] involves summing and integrating over (k_widetildeV, lambda_widetildeV), then tau^-1M-certainly we have the following estimate sqrtUpsiloncdot\|H^circ\|_X_widetildeV^-b_0[kk_Bto k_C]lesssimYcdottau^-thetaprod_lin Bcup CN_l^betaprod_linPN_l^-4varepsilonprod_lin EN_l^8varepsilonprod_pinwidetildeYN_p^-delta^3 prod_f in widetildeV N_f^dcdot big(max_lin CN_lbig)^-beta, which follows from () and bigg(sum_k_widetildeVintdlambda_widetildeVcdotprod_finwidetildeVlanglelambda_frangle^-2b_0prod_j=1^rX_j^*(k_V_j,lambda_V_j)^2bigg)^1/2lesssimprod_j=1^rX_jprod_j=r+1^q N_j^d/2. Note that () follows from taking the tensor product of () for 1leq jleq r and summing and integrating over (k_j,lambda_j) for r+1leq jleq q. Finally, the desired bound () for H_kk_U(k_V,lambda_V) follows from () and () in view of the N_f^-D_1 powers on the right hand side of (). The desired bounds () and () for H_kk_U(k_V,lambda_V) can be obtained in a similar way. Step 2: removing over-pairings. From now on we will fix the value of (k_widetildeV,lambda_widetildeV) and reduce to the setting of the tensor widetildeH in () and the tensor H^circ in (). We will first focus on (), fix a subpartition (B,C) of U with Cneqvarnothing, and denote E=Ubackslash(Bcup C). Recall that O=\A_1,cdots,A_m\ is the collection of all pairings and over-pairings (see Definition ), and notice that the frequencies N_l are the same for linA_i. Without loss of generality, we may assume the frequency N_l for linA_i is geq M^delta for all 1leq ileq v (where 1leq vleq m), and leq M^[delta] for v+1leq ileq m. In particular, we have that A_icapU=varnothing and that A_icap U_1=varnothing for igeq v+1 (since N_lgeq M^delta for linU and linU_1). Next, in (), the product prod_l,l'^(2) has two parts, namely prod_l,l'^(2,geq) containing (l,l') such that N_l=N_l'geq M^delta, and prod_l,l'^(2,<) containing (l,l') such that N_l=N_l'< M^delta. In the proof below we will slightly modify () by changing prod_l,l'^(2) 1_k_lneq k_l' into prod_l,l'^(2,<) 1_k_lneq k_l'. This will be necessary in order to separate the tensor h^(1) from the rest later in the proof, and will not cause a problem, since the original widetildeH equals the modified widetildeH multiplied by prod_l,l'^(2,geq)1_k_lneq k_l', and the original H^circ equals the modified H^circ multiplied by prod_l,l'^(2,geq)1_k_lneq k_l', which is a bounded operation due to Lemma . The reason we need to keep the factors in the product prod_l,l'^(2,<)1_k_lneq k_l' is to guarantee the no-pairing assumption required to apply Proposition later in Step 3. Recall that when Cneqvarnothing we have max\N_l:lin CcapU_1\simmax\N_l:lin C\ (see part (i) in the assumption). Denote the particular lin CcapU_1 where the maximum is attained by l_top. In this step we shall fix the values of k_l for lin E and for lin A_i, where 1leq ileq v and |A_i|geq 3. These l's are divided into groups according to the pairing and over-pairing relations, and there are four possible cases: Case 1: For each lin E that does not belong to any A_i, we form a group with only one element l. Each of these l belongs to a unique U_j for some 1leq jleq r. Case 2: For each i such that A_icap Eneqvarnothing, we form a group containing all elements of this A_i. DefinefootnoteRecall that Q is defined in (). Since Q contains the two-element pairings in A_i, |A_icapQ| is even. y_i and z_i such that |A_icapQ|=2y_i and |A_icapwidetildeU|=z_i. Also note that, the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1,\dagger)}$ and sum $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{Q}^\dagger}}^{(3,\dagger)}$ are exactly the same as the ones defined in (\ref{merge1}) when merging the tensors $(h^{(1,\dagger)},\cdots, h^{(r,\dagger)})$ via $(h,\mathscr{B},\mathscr{O}^\dagger)$.

Let us illustrate the above \emph{Step 2} with an explicit example, which is an extension of the example in \emph{Step 2} of the proof of Proposition \ref{algorithm1}; for simplicity, assume there is no blossoms (i.e. $\mathcal{V}_j=\varnothing$) and all frequencies are $\geq M^\delta$, so no trimming is needed throughout the process. Suppose $q=r=7$, \[(\mathcal{U}_1,\mathcal{U}_2,\cdots,\mathcal{U}_7)= (\{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{j}, \mathfrak{k}, \mathfrak{m}\},\,\{\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{k},\mathfrak{o}\},\,\{\mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{e}, \mathfrak{k}\},\,\{\mathfrak{e}, \mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{g}\},\,\{\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{h}, \mathfrak{j}, \mathfrak{m}\},\,\{\mathfrak{i}, \mathfrak{j}, \mathfrak{k},\mathfrak{m}\},\,\{\mathfrak{k},\mathfrak{m}\}),\] and the corresponding frequencies satisfy \[N_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{a}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{b}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{c}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{d}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{e}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{f}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{g}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{h}} \geq N_{\mathfrak{i}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{j}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{k}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{m}}\geq N_{\mathfrak{o}}\geq M^\delta.\] Like in the proof of Proposition \ref{algorithm1}, a leaf occurring in at least two sets represents a pairing or over-pairing; for these leaves $\mathfrak{l}$, we also use $\mathfrak{l}_j$ to indicate the copy of $\mathfrak{l}$ in $\mathcal{U}_j$. Then $\mathcal{U} =\widetilde{\mathcal{U}} =\{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}},\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h},\mathfrak{i},\mathfrak{j},\mathfrak{k},\mathfrak{o}\}$ and $\widetilde{H}=H^{\circ}$, and
\begin{multline*}(H^\circ)_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}=\sum_{(k_1,\cdots,k_7)}\sum_{(k_{\mathfrak{a}},k_{\mathfrak{c}},k_{\mathfrak{e}},k_{\mathfrak{f}},k_{\mathfrak{m}})}h_{kk_1\cdots k_7}\cdot h^{(1)}_{k_1k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}k_{\mathfrak{c}} k_{\mathfrak{j}} k_{\mathfrak{k}} k_{\mathfrak{m}}}\cdot h^{(2)}_{k_2k_{\mathfrak{a}} k_{\mathfrak{b}} k_{\mathfrak{k}} k_{\mathfrak{o}}}\\\times h^{(3)}_{k_3k_{\mathfrak{c}} k_{\mathfrak{d}} k_{\mathfrak{e}} k_{\mathfrak{k}}}\cdot h^{(4)}_{k_4k_{\mathfrak{e}} k_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{g}}}\cdot h^{(5)}_{k_5k_{\mathfrak{a}} k_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{h}} k_{\mathfrak{j}} k_{\mathfrak{m}}}\cdot h^{(6)}_{k_6 k_{\mathfrak{i}} k_{\mathfrak{j}} k_{\mathfrak{k}} k_{\mathfrak{m}}}\cdot h^{(7)}_{k_7k_{\mathfrak{k}} k_{\mathfrak{m}}},
\end{multline*} where for simplicity,  we have omitted the various $\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}$ factors.

Suppose $B=\{\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{d}\}$ and $C=\{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}},\mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}, \mathfrak{k}\}$ is a subpartition of $\mathcal{U}$ and $E=\{\mathfrak{i}, \mathfrak{j}, \mathfrak{o}\}$.
Our goal is to estimate $\|H^\circ\|_{kk_B\to k_C}$. The groups in \emph{Cases 1--4} in the above process are then:
\begin{itemize}
\item\emph{Case 1}: $\{\mathfrak{i}\}$ and $\{\mathfrak{o}\}$;
\item\emph{Case 2}: $\mathcal{A}_1 =\{\mathfrak{j}_1, \mathfrak{j}_5, \mathfrak{j}_6\}$;
\item\emph{Case 3}: $\mathcal{A}_2 =\{\mathfrak{k}_1, \mathfrak{k}_2, \mathfrak{k}_3,\mathfrak{k}_6,\mathfrak{k}_7\}$;
\item\emph{Case 4}: $\mathcal{A}_3 = \{\mathfrak{m}_1, \mathfrak{m}_5,\mathfrak{m}_6,\mathfrak{m}_7\}$.
\end{itemize}
After fixing the values of $(k_{\mathfrak{i}},k_{\mathfrak{o}},k_{\mathfrak{j}},k_{\mathfrak{k}},k_{\mathfrak{m}})$, which are considered in \emph{Cases 1--4} above, we can reduce $\|H^\circ\|_{kk_B\to k_C}$ to $\|(H^\circ)^\dagger\|_{kk_{B^\dagger}\to k_{C^\dagger}}$ by the above argument, where the relevant sets
\begin{equation}\label{prop6.4:example}
B^\dagger =\{\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{d}\},\,\, C^{\dagger} =\{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}, \mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}\},\,\, \mathcal{U}^\dagger = \{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}},\mathfrak{b},\mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}\},\,\, \mathcal{Q}^{\dagger} =\{\mathfrak{a}_2, \mathfrak{a}_5, \mathfrak{c}_1,\mathfrak{c}_3, \mathfrak{e}_3, \mathfrak{e}_4, \mathfrak{f}_4, \mathfrak{f}_5\},
\end{equation}
\[(\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger,\cdots, \mathcal{U}_7^\dagger)=(\{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}, \mathfrak{c}\},\,\{\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{b}\},\,\{\mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{e}\},\,\{\mathfrak{e}, \mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{g}\},\,\{\mathfrak{a}, \mathfrak{f}, \mathfrak{h}\},\,\varnothing,\,\varnothing),\] and the tensors
\[(H^\circ)_{kk_{\mathcal{U}^\dagger}}^\dagger=\sum_{(k_1,\cdots,k_7)}\sum_{(k_{\mathfrak{a}},k_{\mathfrak{c}},k_{\mathfrak{e}},k_{\mathfrak{f}})}h_{kk_1\cdots k_7}\cdot h^{(1,\dagger)}_{k_1k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}k_{\mathfrak{c}} }\cdot h^{(2,\dagger)}_{k_2k_{\mathfrak{a}} k_{\mathfrak{b}} }\cdot h^{(3,\dagger)}_{k_3k_{\mathfrak{c}} k_{\mathfrak{d}} k_{\mathfrak{e}} }\cdot h^{(4,\dagger)}_{k_4k_{\mathfrak{e}} k_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{g}}}\cdot h^{(5,\dagger)}_{k_5k_{\mathfrak{a}} k_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{h}} }\cdot h^{(6,\dagger)}_{k_6 }\cdot h^{(7,\dagger)}_{k_7},\] where $h_{k_jk_{\mathcal{U}_j^\dagger}}^{(j,\dagger)}$ is $h_{k_jk_{\mathcal{U}_j}}^{(j)}$ after fixing the $k_{\mathcal{U}_j\backslash\mathcal{U}_j^\dagger}$ for $1\leq j\leq 7$.

\emph{Step 3: the method of descent.} Now we need to estimate $(H^\circ)^\dagger$. A key step is to implement Proposition \ref{algorithm1} by singling out $h^{1,\dagger}$. To that effect, consider those $\mathcal{A}_i\in\mathscr{O}^\dagger$ such that $\mathcal{A}_i\cap \mathcal{U}_1^\dagger\neq\varnothing$; we know that each such $\mathcal{A}_i$ contains exactly one pair. Let $(\mathscr{O}^{\dagger})'$ be $\mathscr{O}^\dagger$ after removing these $\mathcal{A}_i$'s, and $\mathcal{D}$ be the union of these $\mathcal{A}_i$'s. Define $\mathcal{F}=(\mathcal{U}^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\backslash\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger$ and similarly define $\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}=(\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\backslash\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger$, so that $\widetilde{\mathcal{U}}^\dagger\backslash \mathcal{U}^\dagger=\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}$.  Then by (\ref{reducedtrim2})--(\ref{reducedmerge2}) we have
\begin{equation}\label{separate}
(H^\circ)_{kk_{\mathcal{U}^\dagger}}^\dagger=\sum_{k_1}\sum_{k_{\mathcal{D}}}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{D}}\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}\cdot\big[h_{k_1k_{\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger}}^{(1,\dagger)}\big]^{\zeta_1}\cdot (H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}},
\end{equation} where $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{D}}}$ is taken over all $k_{\mathcal{D}}$ such that $k_{\mathfrak{l}}=k_{\mathfrak{l}'}$ for any pairing $\mathcal{A}_i=\{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'\}\subset\mathcal{D}$, and the tensor $(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}}$ is defined by
\begin{equation}\label{reducedtrim3}(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}}=\sum_{k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}}}\mathcal{H}_{kk_1k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}}}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}}(f_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}})_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}^{\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}}^*},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}\label{reducedmerge3}\mathcal{H}_{kk_1k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}}}=\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1',\dagger)}\mathbf{1}_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}=k_{\mathfrak{l}'}}\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(2,<)}\mathbf{1}_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}\neq k_{\mathfrak{l}'}}\cdot\sum_{(k_2,\cdots,k_r)}h_{kk_1\cdots k_r}\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}}}^{(3',\dagger)}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{R}}\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}\prod_{j=2}^{r}\big[h_{k_jk_{\mathcal{U}_j^\dagger}}^{(j,\dagger)}\big]^{\zeta_j}.
\end{equation}  Here $\mathcal{R}=\mathcal{Q}^\dagger\backslash\mathcal{D}$; in (\ref{reducedmerge3}) the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(2,<)}$ is the same as the one defined above in \emph{Step 2}, and the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1',\dagger)}$ is the same as $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1,\dagger)}$ defined in (\ref{reducedmerge2}). The sum $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}}}^{(3',\dagger)}$ is the same as $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{Q}^\dagger}}^{(3,\dagger)}$ defined {in (\ref{reducedmerge2})}, except that the sum here does not involve the variables $k_{\mathcal{D}}$. 
The tensor $H^*$ can be understood as a ``partial trimming'' of $\mathcal{H}$ at frequency $M^\delta$, i.e. only the tree part $\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}$ is trimmed.

Note that $N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{\alpha-\theta}\cdot\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}$ is a bounded function of $k_{\mathfrak{l}}$ and can be absorbed into one of the tensors $h^{(1,\dagger)}$  or $H^*$.
Applying Proposition \ref{bilineartensor} to (\ref{separate})
 with $(k_X,k_Y,k_{A_1},k_{A_2})=(kk_{B^\dagger},k_{C^\dagger},k_1k_{\mathcal{U}^\dagger_1},kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}})$, where we combine any two elements in $\mathcal{D}$ that form a pairing into a single element as we did in the proof of Proposition \ref{gausscont}, we obtain
\begin{equation}\label{reducedest2}\|(H^\circ)^\dagger\|_{kk_{B^\dagger}\to k_{C^\dagger}}\lesssim\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{D}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+\theta}\cdot\|h_{k_1k_{\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger}}^{(1,\dagger)}\|_{k_1k_{(B^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\cap\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger}\to k_{C^\dagger\cap \mathcal{U}_1^\dagger}}\cdot\|(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}}\|_{kk_{B^\dagger\cap \mathcal{F}}\to k_1k_{(C^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\cap\mathcal{F}}}.\end{equation}

To estimate $H^*$ in (\ref{reducedest2}) we shall apply Proposition \ref{gausscont}. First recall
 $N_*=\max(N_2,\cdots,N_q)$, and that since the expression (\ref{reducedmerge3}) for $\mathcal{H}$ involves only $h$ and $h^{(j,\dagger)}$ for $2\leq j\leq r$, by assumption this $\mathcal{H}$ \emph{is $\mathcal{B}_{(N_*)^{[\delta]}}$ measurable}. Next note that by assumption $N_{\mathfrak{l}}\geq (N_*)^\delta$ for each $\mathfrak{l}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}$ and that there is no pairing among $k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}}$ in (\ref{reducedtrim3}) in view of the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(2,<)} \mathbf{1}_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}\neq k_{\mathfrak{l}'}}$ in the definition (\ref{reducedmerge3}) of $\mathcal{H}$. Now we apply Proposition \ref{gausscont} to (\ref{reducedtrim3}), setting $(b,c)=(kk_{B^\dagger\cap \mathcal{F}},\,k_1k_{(C^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\cap\mathcal{F}})$, then for some partition $(B_0,C_0)$ of $\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}$ we have $\tau^{-1}M$-certainly that 
\begin{equation}\label{step3}\|(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}}\|_{kk_{B^\dagger\cap \mathcal{F}}\to k_1k_{(C^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\cap\mathcal{F}}}\lesssim(\tau^{-1}M)^\theta\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash\mathcal{F}}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+\theta}\cdot\|\mathcal{H}\|_{kk_S\to k_1k_T},
\end{equation}
where $S=B_0\cup (B^\dagger\cap \mathcal{F})$ and $T=C_0\cup((C^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\cap\mathcal{F})$. Note that $(S,T)$ form a partition of $\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}$ such that $S\supset B^\dagger\cap \mathcal{F}$ and $T\supset (C^\dagger\cup\mathcal{D})\cap\mathcal{F}$.

 

It now remains to estimate $\mathcal{H}$. By applying Lemma \ref{adjustment} we may remove the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(2,<)} \mathbf{1}_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}\neq k_{\mathfrak{l}'}}$ from the definition (\ref{reducedmerge3}). Then, we can repeat the arguments in \emph{Step 2} above, and fix the values of $k_{\mathfrak{l}}$ for $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{A}_i$ with $\mathcal{A}_i\in(\mathscr{O}^\dagger)'$ and $|\mathcal{A}_i|\geq 3$ (where necessarily $i\geq v+1$). Here we only have two cases:

\emph{Case 3}:
 For each $i$ such that $\mathcal{A}_i\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\neq\varnothing$, we form a group containing all elements of this $\mathcal{A}_i$. Define $y_i$ and $z_i$ such that $|\mathcal{A}_i\cap\mathcal{R}|=2y_i$ and $|\mathcal{A}_i\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}|=z_i$, then $|\mathcal{A}_i|=2y_i+z_i$.

\emph{Case 4}: 
For each $i$ such that $\mathcal{A}_i\cap\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}=\varnothing$, we form a group containing all elements of this $\mathcal{A}_i$. Note that in this case $|\mathcal{A}_i|\geq 4$. Define $y_i$ such that $|\mathcal{A}_i|=2y_i$.

As in \emph{Step 2}, we define $G^\dagger$ to be the union of all groups in \emph{Cases 3--4} defined above. Define $(\mathscr{O}^{\dagger\dagger})'$ to be $(\mathscr{O}^{\dagger})'$ after removing the $\mathcal{A}_i$'s involved in \emph{Cases 3--4} above, $\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^\dagger=\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}\backslash G^\dagger$, and similarly define $S^\dagger$, $T^\dagger$ and $\mathcal{R}^\dagger$. We also define $\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}=\mathcal{U}_j^\dagger\backslash G^\dagger$. With these variables $k_{\mathfrak{l}}$ for $\mathfrak{l}\in G^\dagger$ fixed, we can view $\mathcal{H}$ as a tensor depending on $(k,k_1,k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^\dagger})$, and view $h^{(j,\dagger)}$ as a tensor depending on $(k_j,k_{\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}})$. We define $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}=h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}}}^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ to be $h_{kk_{\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger}}}^{(j,\dagger)}$ with the values of $k_{\mathfrak{l}}$ for $\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}_j^\dagger\backslash \mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}=G^\dagger\cap \mathcal{U}_j^\dagger$ fixed. By the same arguments as in \emph{Step 2}, we deduce that
\begin{equation}\label{reducedest3}\|\mathcal{H}\|_{kk_S\to k_1k_T}\lesssim\prod_i^{(\mathscr{O},3,<)}N_{\mathfrak{l}_i}^{(d/2)-2y_i(\alpha-\theta)}\prod_i^{(\mathscr{O},4,<)}N_{\mathfrak{l}_i}^{d-2y_i(\alpha-\theta)}\cdot\sup_{(k_{\mathfrak{l}})}\|(\mathcal{H}^\dagger)_{kk_1k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^\dagger}}\|_{kk_{S^\dagger}\to k_1k_{T^\dagger}},
\end{equation} where the products $\prod_i^{(\mathscr{O},n,<)}$ and the supremum $\sup_{(k_{\mathfrak{l}})}$ are defined in the same way as in \emph{Step 2} above, and
\begin{equation}\label{reducedmerge4}(\mathcal{H}^\dagger)_{kk_1k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^\dagger}}=\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1',\dagger\dagger)}\mathbf{1}_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}=k_{\mathfrak{l}'}}\sum_{(k_2,\cdots,k_r)}h_{kk_1\cdots k_r}\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}^\dagger}}^{(3',\dagger\dagger)}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{R}^\dagger}\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}\prod_{j=2}^{r}\big[h_{k_jk_{\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}}}^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}\big]^{\zeta_j}.
\end{equation} In (\ref{reducedmerge4}) the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1',\dagger\dagger)}$ is the same as $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1',\dagger)}$ defined  in (\ref{reducedmerge3}), except that the product here is only taken over $\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'\in\mathcal{A}_i$ for some $\mathcal{A}_i\in(\mathscr{O}^{\dagger\dagger})'$; similarly, the sum $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}^\dagger}}^{(3',\dagger\dagger)}$ is the same as $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}}}^{(3',\dagger)}$ defined in (\ref{reducedmerge3}), except that the sum here does not involve the variables $k_{\mathcal{R}\backslash\mathcal{R}^\dagger}$. Note that $|\mathcal{A}_i|=2$ and $\mathcal{A}_i\cap \widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^\dagger=\varnothing$ for any $\mathcal{A}_i\in (\mathscr{O}^{\dagger\dagger})'$, so the product $\prod_{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'}^{(1',\dagger\dagger)}$ vacuously equals $1$, and the condition of the sum $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}^\dagger}}^{(3',\dagger\dagger)}$ is just $k_{\mathfrak{l}}=k_{\mathfrak{l}'}$ for each pairing $\{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'\}\in(\mathscr{O}^{\dagger\dagger})'$ (recall that $\mathcal{R}^\dagger = \mathcal{R}\backslash G^\dagger = \mathcal{Q}\backslash (\mathcal{D}\cup G\cup G^\dagger)$).

Now recall the example in \emph{Step 2}. To estimate $\|(H^\circ)^\dagger\|_{kk_{B^\dagger}\to k_{C^\dagger}}$, we separate $h^{(1)}$ from the others as in (\ref{separate})--(\ref{reducedmerge3}), where  $\mathcal{D} = \{\mathfrak{c}_1, \mathfrak{c}_3\}$, $\mathcal{U}_1^\dagger=\{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}, \mathfrak{c}\}$, $\mathcal{F} =\widetilde{\mathcal{F}} =\{\mathfrak{b}, \mathfrak{c}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{g}, \mathfrak{h}\}$ and $\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{Q}^{\dagger}\backslash \mathcal{D}=\{\mathfrak{a}_2,\mathfrak{a}_5,\mathfrak{e}_3,\mathfrak{e}_4,\mathfrak{f}_4,\mathfrak{f}_5\}$, namely
\[(H^\circ)_{kk_{\mathcal{U}^\dagger}}^\dagger=\sum_{k_1,k_{\mathfrak{c}}}h^{(1,\dagger)}_{k_1k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}k_{\mathfrak{c}}}(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}},\]
\[(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}}=\sum_{(k_2,\cdots k_7)}\sum_{(k_{\mathfrak{a}},k_{\mathfrak{e}},k_{\mathfrak{f}})}h_{kk_1\cdots k_7}\cdot h_{k_2k_{\mathfrak{a}} k_{\mathfrak{b}}}^{(2,\dagger)} \cdot h_{k_3k_{\mathfrak{c}} k_{\mathfrak{d}} k_{\mathfrak{e}}}^{(3,\dagger)}\cdot h_{k_4k_{\mathfrak{e}} k_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{g}}}^{(4,\dagger)} \cdot h_{k_5k_{\mathfrak{a}} k_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{h}}}^{(5,\dagger)}\cdot h_{k_6}^{(6,\dagger)}\cdot h_{k_7}^{(7,\dagger)},\]
where for simplicity, we have again omitted the various $\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}$ factors (and also the power factors below). Note that $H^* = \mathcal{H} = \mathcal{H}^{\dagger}$ as all frequencies are $\geq M^\delta$, in particular no partial trimming or \emph{Cases 3--4} in \emph{Step 3} above is involved. By (\ref{reducedest2}) we have
\[
\|(H^\circ)_{kk_{\mathcal{U}^\dagger}}^\dagger\|_{kk_{\mathfrak{b}} k_{\mathfrak{d}}\to k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}k_{\mathfrak{g}} k_{\mathfrak{h}}}\leq\|h^{(1,\dagger)}_{k_1k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}k_{\mathfrak{c}}}\|_{k_1k_{\mathfrak{c}}\to k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}}\cdot
\|(H^*)_{kk_1k_{\mathcal{F}}}\|_{kk_{\mathfrak{b}} k_{\mathfrak{d}}\to k_1k_{\mathfrak{c}}k_{\mathfrak{g}}k_{\mathfrak{h}}}.
\] The norm $\|h^{(1,\dagger)}\|_{k_1k_{\mathfrak{c}}\to k_{\mathfrak{l}_{\mathrm{top}}}}$ is then controlled using (\ref{boundmerge1})--(\ref{boundmerge3}), and $\|H^*\|_{kk_{\mathfrak{b}} k_{\mathfrak{d}}\to k_1k_{\mathfrak{c}}k_{\mathfrak{g}}k_{\mathfrak{h}}}$ is controlled using Proposition \ref{algorithm1}; note that here $\mathcal{E}=\{6,7\}$ as in the example in \emph{Step 2} of the proof of Proposition \ref{algorithm1}, and the corresponding $H^{\mathrm{sg}}$ is the same as the one in that example, but with $h^{(j)}$ replaced by $h^{(j,\dagger)}$. After putting these two bounds together and calculating the various powers involved (see \emph{Step 4}), we can obtain the desired estimate (\ref{boundmerge7}) for this example.

\emph{Step 4: putting together.} We now need to estimate $\mathcal{H}^\dagger$. As in \emph{Step 3}, we may replace $\Delta_{N_{\mathfrak{l}}}\gamma_{k_{\mathfrak{l}}}$ by $N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+\theta}$ and absorb the resulting factor into one of the tensors $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ using Lemma \ref{adjustment}, so instead of $\mathcal{H}^\dagger$ we only need to consider
\begin{equation}\label{reducedmerge5}\mathcal{M}_{kk_1k_{\widetilde{\mathcal{F}}^\dagger}}:=\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{R}^\dagger}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-\alpha+\theta}\sum_{(k_2,\cdots,k_r)}h_{kk_1\cdots k_r}\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}^\dagger}}\prod_{j=2}^{r}\big[h_{k_jk_{\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}}}^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}\big]^{\zeta_j},
\end{equation} where $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}^\dagger}}$ is the sum such that $k_{\mathfrak{l}}=k_{\mathfrak{l}'}$ for each pairing $\{\mathfrak{l},\mathfrak{l}'\}\in (\mathscr{O}^{\dagger\dagger})'$  which is just $\sum_{k_{\mathcal{R}^\dagger}}^{(3',\dagger\dagger)}$ in (\ref{reducedmerge4}). We shall apply Proposition \ref{algorithm1} to estimate (\ref{reducedmerge5}), but we first need to make a few adjustments to fit the framework of (\ref{defH})--(\ref{outputbd}).

First, for $r+1\leq j\leq q$, we may define $\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}=\varnothing$ and $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}=h_{k_j}^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ be supported at a single point $k_j$ (the one fixed in \emph{Step 1}).  Moreover, in view of the extra factor  $\prod_{j=r+1}^q N_j^{-d/2}$ described in \emph{Step 1} when stating the norm bounds we want to prove for $H_{kk_{\mathcal{U}}}^\circ$, we may assume $|h_{k_j}^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}|\lesssim N_j^{-d/2}$ for $r+1\leq j\leq q$, so it satisfies the type $R0^+$ conditions\footnote{The support condition (\ref{type1+}) for type $R0^+$ can be immediately verified, since $\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger} = \varnothing$.} of Proposition \ref{algorithm1} with $\mathfrak{X}_j$ replaced by $1$.
Second, we also view $h_{kk_1\cdots k_r}$ as a tensor depending on $(k,k_1,\cdots,k_q$), in the support of which $k_j\,(r+1\leq j\leq q)$ takes a single value, and denote it by $h_{kk_1\cdots k_q}$. Moreover, the tensor $h=h_{kk_1\cdots k_q}$ satisfies the support condition (\ref{tensorsupport}) for some choice of $\Gamma$, as well as other conditions of $h$ listed in Proposition \ref{algorithm1}. 

Next we check that $h_{k_jk_{\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}}}^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ for $2\leq j\leq r$ satisfy the conditions in Proposition \ref{algorithm1}.
Note that $\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}$ is a subset of $\mathcal{U}_j$, and $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ is formed from $h^{(j)}$ by fixing the values of $k_{\mathcal{U}_j\backslash\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}}$ (for simplicity we denote it by $k_{G_j}$, where $G_j = \mathcal{U}_j\backslash\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}= (G\cap \mathcal{U}_j)\cup (G^\dagger\cap \mathcal{U}_j)$). We consider the following scenarios.

\emph{Scenario 1}: when $h^{(j)}$ has type 1. Then $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ will have type $R1$ in the sense of Proposition \ref{algorithm1}. Indeed by (\ref{boundmerge5}) (actually the modified version of it\footnote{In the analogous sense that (\ref{eq:modified6.40}) is the modified version of (\ref{boundmerge2}).} in \emph{Step 1}), we may assume
\[\bigg|k_j-\sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{U}_j}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}-\ell_j\bigg|\leq (N_*)^{3\delta},\quad \ell_j=\sum_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}_j}\zeta_{\mathfrak{f}} k_{\mathfrak{f}},\] otherwise we gain a huge power of $M$ from (\ref{boundmerge5}) that would suffice (note that $\kappa\gg_{C_\delta}1$ and $N_*\geq M^\delta$). When $k_{G_j}$ is fixed, the above implies that $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ satisfies (\ref{type2}) with $\mathcal{U}_j$ replaced by $\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}$ and some fixed $m_j= \ell_j + \sum_{\mathfrak{l}\in G_j}\zeta_{\mathfrak{l}} k_{\mathfrak{l}}$. Moreover, by (\ref{boundmerge2})--(\ref{boundmerge3}) we deduce that $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}$ satisfies (\ref{type2bd2}) with $\mathcal{U}_j$ replaced by $\mathcal{U}_j^{\dagger\dagger}$, and $\mathfrak{X}_j$ replaced by
\[\mathfrak{X}_j^*\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{P}_j}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-4\varepsilon}\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in G_j}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{8\varepsilon}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\in\mathcal{Y}_j}N_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-\delta^3}\prod_{\mathfrak{f}\in\mathcal{V}_j}N_{\mathfrak{f}}^d.\]

\emph{Scenario 2}: when $h^{(j)}$ has type 0, and $G_j=\varnothing$. Then in this case, $h^{(j,\dagger\dagger)}=h^{(j)}$  and it will have type $R0$ in the sense of Proposition \ref{algorithm1}. It satisfies (\ref{type1bd1})--(\ref{type1bd2}) with $\mathfrak{X}_j$ replaced by
\begin{equation}\label{newadd1}\mathfrak{X}_j^*\cdot\prod_{\mathfrak{l}\in\mathcal{P}_j}N_{\mathfrak{l}}^{-4\varepsilon}\prod_{\mathfrak{p}\in\mathcal{Y}_j}N_{\mathfrak{p}}^{-\delta^3}.\end{equation}

\[\mathscr{L}^{M,\zeta}=\mathscr{L}^{M,M^{[\delta]},\zeta}=\sum_{L<M^\delta}\widetilde{\mathscr{L}}^{ML,\zeta},\]
